ANOVA (Analysis of Variance): Compares means across groups for 1 continuous dependent variable.
ANCOVA (Analysis of Covariance): Compares group means on 1 continuous outcome while adjusting for covariate(s).
MANOVA (Multivariate ANOVA): Compares group means across 2+ continuous dependent variables simultaneously.
MANCOVA (Multivariate ANCOVA): Compares group means across 2+ continuous outcome variables while adjusting for covariate(s).

ANOVA (Analysis of Variance): Statistical method to test if 3+ independent group means differ significantly.
ANCOVA (Analysis of Covariance): Extension of ANOVA that blends ANOVA and linear regression to control for a continuous nuisance variable.
MANOVA (Multivariate ANOVA): Extension of ANOVA that evaluates differences across groups on multiple interrelated dependent variables.
MANCOVA (Multivariate ANCOVA): Extension combining MANOVA and ANCOVA to evaluate multiple dependent variables while controlling for covariate(s).

ANOVA (Analysis of Variance): When comparing 3 or more group means on a single metric to see if at least one group differs.
ANCOVA (Analysis of Covariance): When a continuous baseline/confounding variable influences the outcome and needs to be statistically controlled.
MANOVA (Multivariate ANOVA): When outcomes are correlated or when evaluating a multi-faceted construct across group conditions.
MANCOVA (Multivariate ANCOVA): When studying multi-faceted outcomes where continuous baseline/confounding variables must be controlled.

ANOVA (Analysis of Variance): Reduces Type I error compared to running multiple two-sample t-tests; straightforward interpretation.
ANCOVA (Analysis of Covariance): Increases statistical power and reduces unexplained error variance by statistically removing noise caused by covariates.
MANOVA (Multivariate ANOVA): Controls for experiment-wise error rate across multiple outcomes; detects multi-outcome patterns invisible in univariate tests.
MANCOVA (Multivariate ANCOVA): Highest statistical precision for multi-outcome designs; accounts for both outcome interrelationships and extraneous noise.

Feature / Dimension: Sequential Steps in the Analysis Process
Identify Independent Variables (factors), Dependent Variables, and continuous Covariates.
Verify measurement scales (Categorical IVs, Continuous DVs/Covariates).
Test for normality (Shapiro-Wilk) and homogeneity of variances (Levene's Test).
For MANOVA/MANCOVA: Test Box's M for covariance equality and check correlation matrix among DVs ($0.2 < \vert{}r\vert{} < 0.8$).
For ANCOVA/MANCOVA: Test the interaction between IV and Covariate to ensure homogeneity of regression slopes.
MANOVA/MANCOVA: Evaluate multivariate test statistics (Wilks' Lambda, Pillai's Trace, Hotelling's Trace, or Roy's Largest Root).
If significant, conduct post-hoc pairwise comparisons (e.g., Tukey's HSD or Bonferroni adjustments) or univariate ANOVAs following a MANOVA.
Covariate Timing (ANCOVA & MANCOVA): Measure covariates before applying experimental treatments to ensure the IV does not alter the covariate.
Homogeneity of Regression Slopes: If the IV and Covariate interact significantly, the ANCOVA model is invalid; use a moderated regression approach instead.
Multicollinearity in DVs (MANOVA & MANCOVA): Highly correlated outcome variables ($r > 0.85$ or $0.90$) introduce instability into matrix inversion; drop redundant DVs or combine them.
Sample Size Considerations: MANOVA and MANCOVA require larger sample sizes per cell (ideally more observations per cell than the number of DVs + Covariates) to maintain adequate statistical power.
